introduction: On this Sunday, Elisha leaves his plow and his oxen to follow Elijah. In the Gospel, Jesus sets his face toward Jerusalem, and he tells those who want to follow him that the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head, and that no one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the Kingdom of God. Paul tells us that Christ has set us free for love. Let us follow Jesus without looking back.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Lord is our portion and our cup. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may follow Christ with determination and freedom. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are discerning a call to the priesthood or religious life: that they may answer generously and without looking back. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who meet hostility or rejection: that, like Jesus, they may respond with patience and not with violence. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the homeless and all who have nowhere to lay their heads: that they may find shelter and care. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may use our freedom not for selfishness, but to serve one another in love. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, your Son set his face toward Jerusalem to fulfill your will. Give us the freedom to follow him without looking back, and to serve one another in love. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: He set his face to go to Jerusalem
reflection.body:
Elijah finds Elisha plowing a field with twelve yoke of oxen and throws his cloak over him. It is a call. Elisha asks for time to say goodbye to his parents. Then he does something decisive: he slaughters the oxen, burns the plow to cook the meat, gives it to the people, and follows Elijah. He leaves no way back.

In the Gospel, Luke marks a turning point: "when the days were near that he should be taken up, he intently set his face to go to Jerusalem." From here on, the whole Gospel is a journey toward the cross.

Along the way, a Samaritan village refuses to welcome Jesus. James and John want to call down fire from heaven on it. Jesus rebukes them. His way is not revenge.

Then three people talk about following him. To the first, who promises to follow him anywhere, Jesus says, "The foxes have holes and the birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay his head." Following Jesus means giving up security. The second wants first to bury his father, and Jesus answers, "Leave the dead to bury their own dead, but you go and announce God's Kingdom." The third wants to say goodbye at home, and Jesus says, "No one, having put his hand to the plow and looking back, is fit for God's Kingdom." These are hard words. They tell us that nothing, not even good things, should come before Christ.

Paul speaks of the freedom Christ gives: "Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free." But this freedom is for love: "through love be servants to one another."

This week, ask yourself what you keep looking back at. Set your face toward the Lord, and follow him freely.
